aztec_tlaltecuhtli.name: Devour blood and the dead to renew the earth
aztec_tlaltecuhtli.notes: Insatiable earth-monster who must be sated with human hearts and blood lest she withhold the earth's bounty and the crops fail.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

aztec_tonatiuh.name: Rule the east and the daytime sky as lord of warriors
aztec_tonatiuh.notes: Solar deity governing the cardinal east, into whose paradise fallen warriors and sacrificed captives ascend as escorts of the sun.

aztec_xipe_totec.name: Patronize goldsmiths and the working of precious metal
aztec_xipe_totec.notes: Tutelary god of the metalworkers' guild; the golden flayed skin he wears is read as the gilding of the goldsmith's craft.

aztec_xipe_totec.name: Preside over gladiatorial (striping) sacrifice
aztec_xipe_totec.notes: Patron of the gladiatorial combat in which a tethered captive fought armed warriors at the festival Tlacaxipehualiztli.

aztec_xochiquetzal.name: Govern flowers, beauty, sexual pleasure and love
aztec_xochiquetzal.notes: Goddess of flowers, female sexual power, pleasure and youthful beauty, attended by butterflies and birds.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

babalu_aye.name: Send and withdraw plague at will
babalu_aye.notes: As the Yoruba lord of smallpox and epidemic disease, he both looses and stays pestilence; in one legend he swept sesame seeds into the air to create fever and smallpox.

sources.reference: Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief

balinese_batara_guru.name: Uphold cosmic order from Mount Meru as king of the gods
balinese_batara_guru.notes: As the Balinese-Javanese form of Shiva (Rudra), he rules the heaven Kahyangan and oversees the order of the three worlds.

sources.reference: Hooykaas, Cosmogony and Creation in Balinese Tradition

balinese_dewi_danu.name: Rule Lake Batur as the source of Bali's rivers and springs
balinese_dewi_danu.notes: Lake-goddess from whom the island's irrigation water flows; in myth she rose from the crater lake and poured sacred water from a golden jug to revive the parched land.

sources.reference: Lansing, Priests and Programmers: Technologies of Power in the Engineered Landscape of Bali

balinese_rangda.name: Devour children and prey on the newborn
balinese_rangda.notes: Child-eating demon-queen who threatens infants and the unborn, balanced eternally against the protective Barong.

balinese_sedana.name: Grant gold, silver, money and good fortune to traders
balinese_sedana.notes: God of wealth (dana = wealth/money) revered by merchants and businessmen, equated with the prosperity of Lakshmi; consort of Dewi Sri.

bambara_ndomadyiri.name: Separate and distinguish things, giving creation its order
bambara_ndomadyiri.notes: Heavenly blacksmith whose principal task is to part and define beings, rendering the thought of creation into an articulate order.

sources.reference: Dieterlen, Essai sur la religion bambara

bambara_mousso_koroni.name: Work the first sorcery as the original mistress of magic
bambara_mousso_koroni.notes: Reckoned the first sorcerer; in her jealousy she planted Pemba in the earth and roamed the world sowing wanzo, the feminine force of impurity later excised from the body in circumcision.

sources.reference: Dieterlen, Essai sur la religion bambara

bambara_mousso_koroni.name: Introduce disorder, illness and death to humankind
bambara_mousso_koroni.notes: Wandering the world she brought confusion, sickness and mortality, the disordering counterpart to Faro's ordering of creation.

banyaruanda_imana.name: Bestow good fortune, fertility and children as Habyarimana
banyaruanda_imana.notes: Sole giver of offspring and prosperity; his 'very long arms' reach down to rescue and bless even where he remains remote from daily cult.

sources.reference: Maquet, The Premise of Inequality in Ruanda

banyaruanda_nkuba.name: Hurl the thunderbolt as King of the Sky
banyaruanda_nkuba.notes: The Lightning, titled Umwami wo Hejuru ('King of the Sky'), celestial sovereign and apex of the Ibimanuka royal ancestry.

sources.reference: d'Hertefelt & Coupez, La royauté sacrée de l'ancien Rwanda

basque_basajaun.name: Keep the secret of cereal cultivation as the first farmer
basque_basajaun.notes: The forest lords first knew how to sow wheat and the calendar of planting; the trickster San Martin Txiki stole the secret of grain, the saw and iron-soldering from them for humankind.

basque_aatxe.name: Enforce the will of Mari, punishing cheats and wrongdoers
basque_aatxe.notes: Read as an agent or guise of the goddess Mari, the red bull-spirit punishes criminals and those who defraud her.

basque_eguzki.name: Return nightly through the red seas into the Earth-mother's womb
basque_eguzki.notes: Daughter of Amalur, the Sun sinks each evening through Itxasgorrieta ('the reddish seas') back into the earth from which she is reborn.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

aztec_tezcatlipoca.name: Toxcatl
aztec_tezcatlipoca.notes: A flawless youth was chosen a year ahead to live as the god's living image (ixiptla), feasted, given four wives, and at the festival climbed the temple breaking flutes step by step before being sacrificed.

aztec_tlaloc.name: Atlcahualo / Mount Tlaloc rites
aztec_tlaloc.notes: Children were sacrificed to the rain-lord at hilltop shrines and at the boulder-shrine atop Mount Tlaloc to open the rainy season; he shared the summit of the Templo Mayor with Huitzilopochtli.

aztec_tonatiuh.name: Solar offering of hearts and blood
aztec_tonatiuh.notes: The sun's daily motion was held to depend on the heart-blood of sacrificed captives, sustained by the militaristic warrior cults.

aztec_xipe_totec.name: Tlacaxipehualiztli
aztec_xipe_totec.notes: 'The Flaying of Men': captives were sacrificed and gladiatorially fought, then flayed, their skins worn by penitents for twenty days until they rotted, enacting the husking and renewal of the seed.

aztec_xiuhtecuhtli.name: New Fire Ceremony
aztec_xiuhtecuhtli.notes: At the close of each calendar round all fires were extinguished and a new fire kindled in the breast of a sacrificed captive on the Hill of the Star, then carried to rekindle the hearths of the land; the fire-lord was also feasted at Izcalli.

aztec_tlazolteotl.name: Ochpaniztli
aztec_tlazolteotl.notes: The 'Sweeping of the Roads': a great autumn cleansing of the earth-mother goddesses in which streets and houses were swept clear of impurity; her impersonator was sacrificed and flayed.

aztec_xochiquetzal.name: Xochilhuitl (Feast of Flowers)
aztec_xochiquetzal.notes: A flower-festival in which houses, streets and temples were decked with blossoms; women artisans offered their weaving and embroidery to the goddess.

sources.reference: Mexicolore, Goddess of the Month: Xochiquetzal

babalu_aye.name: San Lázaro pilgrimage / awán
babalu_aye.notes: In West Africa his Sopona priesthood monopolised the appeasement of smallpox with sacrifice and herbal cure; in the diaspora tens of thousands process to the church of San Lázaro at El Rincón, and the awán rite encircles a sackcloth basket with plates of food. Sacrifices include the goat, cock and guinea-fowl; toasted corn and palm-oiled popcorn are offered.

balinese_barong.name: Barong–Rangda exorcistic dance-drama
balinese_barong.notes: Sacred dance, accompanied by the gamelan bebarongan, in which the Barong battles Rangda; entranced men turn their krises on themselves and are protected by the Barong's power, restoring the village's balance and health.

balinese_dewi_danu.name: Pakelem at Pura Ulun Danu Batur
balinese_dewi_danu.notes: Subak farmers from across Bali bring offerings to the lake-temple of Dewi Danu, who allocates irrigation water; in the Pakelem rite a water-buffalo is offered into the lake.

balinese_dewi_sri.name: Cili first-fruits and rice rites
balinese_dewi_sri.notes: Woven cili effigies of the goddess are set in the paddy at planting and in the granary at harvest; offerings of coloured rice, betel and coins are made to secure the crop.

balinese_sedana.name: Buda Cemeng Klau (Rambut Sedana)
balinese_sedana.notes: On Buda Wage Klau merchants and households honour the wealth-deity Rambut Sedana, with an annual 'wedding' of Sri and Sedana sought for both harvest and material plenty.

banyaruanda_ryangombe.name: Kubandwa possession cult
banyaruanda_ryangombe.notes: Initiates were 'possessed' by the imandwa-spirits under a godparent's guidance, baptised with an imandwa-name, and feasted with sorghum beer (ikigage); the initiated dwell after death on the volcano Karisimbi. Ryangombe was honoured as king-spirit and mediator before Imana, not worshipped as a god.

sources.reference: de Heusch, Le Rwanda et la civilisation interlacustre

banyaruanda_gihanga.name: The perpetual royal fire and the drum Kalinga
banyaruanda_gihanga.notes: The fire of Gihanga was kept burning without interruption at the royal court 'where the cattle are milked', and his sacred drum Kalinga and long-horned cattle were tended by hereditary ritual families as emblems of the kingship.

basque_mari.name: Cave-offerings to the Lady of Anboto
basque_mari.notes: Petitioners left coins, flowers, candles or a ram at the mouths of her caves, approaching her with deference; she brewed weather from her mountain and punished lying, theft and pride.

attributes.name: Plumed serpent body sheathed in quetzal feathers
attributes.notes: His characteristic form is a serpent clothed in the iridescent green plumes of the quetzal; the earliest cult image stands on the temple façade at Teotihuacan.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

attributes.name: Ehecailacacozcatl, the spirally cut conch wind-jewel
attributes.notes: As Ehecatl he wears the cross-sectioned conch breastplate read as the spiral of wind and whirlpool.

attributes.name: Obsidian smoking-mirror replacing a foot (and at brow or chest)
attributes.notes: He is shown with a smoking obsidian mirror in place of one foot and another at the temple or breast, instrument of his all-seeing scrying.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya
Olivier, Mockeries and Metamorphoses of an Aztec God: Tezcatlipoca
Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

attributes.name: Goggle eyes and jaguar fangs formed of entwined serpents
attributes.notes: Two intertwined serpents loop around the eyes to make rings and form the nose, with long fangs over the lip.

attributes.name: Heron-feather headdress and blue mask
attributes.notes: He wears a fan of white heron feathers above the blue rain-mask.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

attributes.name: Squatting birth-giving pose with splayed limbs
attributes.notes: Carved on the undersides of monuments in a hocker (birthing) posture, clawed and fanged, wearing a skirt of crossbones and skulls; the great Templo Mayor monolith shows blood streaming from her mouth.

attributes.name: Rayed solar disk framing a red face
attributes.notes: Painted red, his face is set in the centre of a rayed sun-disk; on the Calendar Stone his tongue is a sacrificial flint knife.

attributes.name: Suit of flayed human skin over the wearer's red body
attributes.notes: Shown clad in a golden-yellow flayed skin laced up the back, the loose hands of the victim's skin dangling at the wrists, his own red skin visible through the mouth and eyes.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

attributes.name: Roseate-spoonbill feather adornments and golden jewellery
attributes.notes: His impersonator was decked in bright red spoonbill plumes and gold, marking his patronage of the goldsmiths.

attributes.name: Turquoise xiuhtototl bird at the brow and Xiuhcoatl fire-serpent on the back
attributes.notes: Yellow-bodied with a red ring at the mouth, he wears the descending turquoise cotinga on his forehead and bears the fire-serpent Xiuhcoatl across his back.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

attributes.name: Black rubber paint about the mouth and a half-moon nose-plug
attributes.notes: Her lips and chin are smeared with black liquid rubber and she wears a crescent yacametztli nose-ornament, marking the earth-threshold of birth and death.

sources.reference: Miller & Taube, An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya

attributes.name: Headdress of raw unspun cotton with spindles
attributes.notes: Bands of raw cotton bearing weaving spindles crown her, tying her to spinning, weaving and the transformation of the raw into the finished.

sources.reference: Mexicolore, Goddess of the Month: Tlazolteotl

attributes.name: Crown of quetzal-plume flowers over braided red leather
attributes.notes: Flowers in her hair and a garland from which green quetzal feathers rise like horns, with a flowered cotton huipil.

sources.reference: Mexicolore, Goddess of the Month: Xochiquetzal
Mexicolore, Goddess of the Month: Xochiquetzal
Mexicolore, Goddess of the Month: Xochiquetzal

attributes.name: Stooped, sore-covered body wrapped in raffia or sackcloth
attributes.notes: Depicted as a hunched old man scarred by smallpox, his afflicted body hidden under raffia-palm fibre or burlap, sometimes purple in his Saint-Lazarus guise.

sources.reference: Murphy, Santería: African Spirits in America

attributes.name: Composite lion-mask (Barong Ket) with frangipani-decked beard
attributes.notes: The most sacred form, the Barong Ket, has a face compounded of lion, tiger, cow and goat; its power resides in the beard of human hair hung with frangipani, animated by two dancers in a gilded harness.

attributes.name: Fanged, goggle-eyed mask with pendulous breasts, claws and lolling tongue
attributes.notes: A naked hag with wild white hair, tusk-fangs, bulging eyes, drooping breasts and clawed hands, her flame-carved tongue (Lidah Api) hanging to the chest; her white-black-red colours echo Durga.

attributes.name: Very long arms reaching down to mankind
attributes.notes: Pictured as a benevolent being with 'very long arms' able to snatch a person from death, yet otherwise remote, with no temples raised to him.

sources.reference: Maquet, The Premise of Inequality in Ruanda

attributes.name: Woman with a full moon behind her head
attributes.notes: Often shown as a richly dressed lady with the full moon at her back; in Soule she takes the form of a vulture, and crossing the sky she trails fire.

sacredAnimals.name: Ram (her favourite animal, beside her cave)

attributes.name: Beautiful long-haired woman with the webbed feet of a duck (or a fish-tail at sea)
attributes.notes: From the waist up a lovely woman combing her hair, below the webbed feet of a duck or bird's talons; coastal itsaslamiak bear a mermaid's tail.

attributes.name: Golden comb at the water's edge
attributes.notes: Forever seen combing her hair with a golden comb by river, spring or fountain.

attributes.name: Towering hair-covered man of the woods with long beard
attributes.notes: A huge humanoid furred all over, with a beard and hair sometimes reaching the feet; guardian of flocks who whistles to warn shepherds of coming storms.
